title: CQRS
description: Learn about Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS). Understand when to separate read and write models for scalability and performance.

data.text: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates read and write operations into different models. This separation allows you to optimize each model independently for its specific use case.
In traditional CRUD, the same model handles both reads and writes. CQRS splits this into two separate models: a write model for commands and a read model for queries.

items: Commands (writes): Modify state, return no data
Queries (reads): Return data, don't modify state
Separate models for commands and queries
Separate databases or schemas for each model
Synchronization between models via events

data.title: Key Insight
data.text: Read and write operations have very different characteristics. Optimizing them separately allows better performance and scalability.

items.title: Read Optimization
items.description: Read models can be denormalized for fast queries. No complex joins, no write concerns. Optimized for specific query patterns.

items.title: Write Optimization
items.description: Write models focus on business rules and validation. No read performance concerns. Optimized for transactional integrity.

items.title: Independent Scaling
items.description: Scale read and write infrastructure separately. Read-heavy systems can add read replicas without affecting writes.

items.title: Security
items.description: Separate security rules for reads and writes. Some users can read but not write, or vice versa.

items: Simple CQRS: Same database, separate code models
CQRS with Event Sourcing: Write model is event log, read model is projection
Separate databases: Different databases for reads and writes
Synchronization: Events or polling to keep models in sync
Eventual consistency: Read model lags behind write model

data.title: Complexity Trade-off
data.text: CQRS adds significant complexity. Only use it when you have a clear need for separate optimization of reads and writes.

items: High read/write ratio with different access patterns
Complex business logic for writes but simple reads
Need to scale reads and writes independently
Domain with complex validation rules
When read performance is critical
Simple CRUD applications
When read and write patterns are similar
When the team isn't experienced with the pattern
When the added complexity isn't justified
When immediate consistency is required
Start simple—separate code before separating databases
Monitor the lag between write and read models
Design read models for specific query needs
Keep write model focused on business rules
Document the synchronization strategy
Test failure scenarios in synchronization
